title: Cliff Fletcher, Maple Leafs adviser and longtime NHL team executive, dies at 90
content:
Cliff Fletcher, the longtime NHL executive who led the Calgary Flames to the 1989 Stanley Cup, has died at age 90, the Toronto Maple Leafs announced Friday.

Known as Silver Fox and Trader Cliff for his shock of white hair and proclivity for pulling off blockbuster deals, Fletcher had a long association with the Maple Leafs. His tenure included a six-year run as president and general manager between 1991 and 1997, when the team made two trips to the conference finals, and a brief return as GM in 2008.

In addition to the Leafs and Flames, Fletcher also spent time as a scout or executive with the Montreal Canadiens, St. Louis Blues, Atlanta Flames, Tampa Bay Lightning and Phoenix Coyotes in an unmatched front-office career that stretched for more than 70 years.

“Few men in the history of hockey have had as profound and lasting an impact on the game as Cliff Fletcher,” NHL commissioner Gary Bettman said in a statement released by the league. “… On a personal level, Cliff was a friend and trusted advisor upon whom I relied for his wisdom and generous counsel. The entire National Hockey League family mourns his passing and sends its deepest condolences to Linda, his children Chuck and Kristy, and his many friends and admirers throughout the hockey world.”

Fletcher was most recently employed as a senior adviser for the Leafs, a role he held from 2009 until his death.

Born George Clifford Fletcher in Montreal on Aug. 16, 1935, Fletcher began working as a junior scout for the Canadiens while only 21 years old. In his early 30s, he was named assistant GM to the expansion Blues, who made the Stanley Cup Final three years in a row after entering the NHL.

In 1972, Fletcher was named GM of the expansion Atlanta franchise, and he followed the Flames to Calgary when they relocated in 1980. There, they became a top team that was long overshadowed by the rival Edmonton Oilers, culminating in the Flames winning their first and only championship in 1989.

The long-struggling Leafs then airlifted in Fletcher to change their fortunes, and he ushered in one of the most memorable periods in franchise history. In two of his early moves, he hired Pat Burns as head coach and acquired captain Doug Gilmour in a massive 10-player trade with Calgary. Under Fletcher, the Leafs set franchise records for wins and points and had their longest run of playoff success since their 1960s heyday.

Fletcher was inducted into the Hockey Hall of Fame as a builder in 2004. He is survived by his two children, Chuck and Kristy. Chuck Fletcher is also a longtime NHL executive, having previously served as general manager of the Minnesota Wild and Philadelphia Flyers.
